claims.text: A nanocrystalline chromium coating applied by physical vapor deposition can improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding.
The chromium coating can retain suitability for service without compromising cladding performance.
The coating forms a dense Cr2O3 scale on its surface under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The resulting Cr2O3 scale adheres to the chromium coating.
The Cr2O3 scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Chromium in the coating preferentially oxidizes to Cr2O3 at high temperature.
The Cr2O3 scale is thermodynamically stable under the proposed high-temperature conditions.
Reduced oxygen ingress through the Cr2O3 scale retards oxidation of the underlying zirconium alloy.
The Cr2O3 scale may self-heal minor damage.
The coating extends the time before rapid oxidation and degradation occur.
Coated cladding will exhibit significantly lower oxidation rates than uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The coating will measurably slow oxidation kinetics relative to uncoated cladding.
The coating is expected to remain effective in steam or air at temperatures near 1200 degrees Celsius.
The degree of oxidation-resistance improvement may depend on coating thickness, scale-formation dynamics, and reactor operating conditions.
